entities.summary:
John O'Sullivan (born Daniel Larkin, 1902–1990) was an Australian civil engineer whose visionary leadership and technical prowess were instrumental in the mid-20th century's most ambitious infrastructure project, the Snowy Mountains Scheme. As the scheme's first Commissioner from 1949 to 1967, O'Sullivan transformed a complex hydrological vision into a tangible reality, harnessing the waters of the Snowy River for both irrigation and hydroelectric power generation. His work profoundly reshaped Australia's economic landscape and national identity during the post-war boom, establishing a model for large-scale engineering and multicultural collaboration that transcended national boundaries.

Educated at the University of Sydney, O'Sullivan gained extensive experience in water management and construction before his pivotal appointment to the Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Authority. Under his stewardship, the scheme involved the construction of 16 major dams, 7 power stations, and 145 kilometers of tunnels, diverting the Snowy River inland to the Murrumbidgee and Murray Rivers. He oversaw an unprecedented recruitment drive, attracting over 100,000 workers from more than 30 nations, integrating them into a cohesive workforce that overcame immense geographical and logistical challenges in the rugged Australian Alps. This period saw the deployment of innovative tunneling techniques and large-scale concrete pouring, pushing the boundaries of contemporary civil engineering.
